metadata.description: Optimal node-to-customer lanes by mode, nearest-node comparison and SLA exceptions.

storymap.title: Which site should serve each customer?
storymap.subtitle: Optimal source by landed cost within SLA
storymap.footer: Illustrative sample data. Site locations approximate; customers, suppliers, volumes and rates are invented.

chapters.title: Every customer, served from the right node
chapters.description:
Each arc is the lowest-cost option that still meets the customer's SLA, coloured by mode: ground, express air, international air.

97.9% of customers within SLA · 1.2 d average transit · $33,665 weekly freight · 4,265 kg CO₂e.

Sample data: Nova sites from the ERP/CRM footprint (locations approximate); customers, suppliers, volumes and rates are illustrative.

chapters.title: Nearest is often not optimal
chapters.description:
For 34 of 47 customers the best source is not the closest node, mainly because product families are stocked at different sites.

Boston: nearest is NOR, but it ships from BIL-E (Ground, 1 day). Nearest node (NOR) does not stock CC.

chapters.title: Mode selection on long lanes
chapters.description: Dallas lab: Nearest node (CAN) does not stock OSM. It ships Express air from NOR in 1 day(s), because ground would miss the 3-day SLA.

chapters.title: The structural gap: South Korea
chapters.description:
Seoul is the one customer outside SLA. The Japan node serves Japan only, so the best option is WIM by International air: 4 days against a 3-day SLA.

A Korea or Taipei stocking point would close the gap.
